chapter_theme: The last twenty verses of Innaa Narpathu each count four painful things, mixing bodily dangers, failures of skill and learning, faults of speech and friendship, and the pains of poverty and patronage, so that a moral fault is weighed on the same scale as a snake in the house or a stone in the areca nut.

21.reading: The verse counts four painful things: giving to people who are not content with the way they were given to, going to eat with those who do not share their food, sickness that comes in old age, and the word of a brahmin who lacks Vedic recitation.
21.nuance: The first two items look at the shared meal from both ends, the gift wasted on the ungrateful and the guest at a house that does not share. The fourth is a birth-rank norm: the brahmin is measured by his ஓத்து (printed ஒத்து), and his speech without it is counted a pain, not an authority.

items.claim: giving to those who are not pleased with the manner of the gift is painful
going to eat at the house of those who do not share their food is painful
sickness when one has grown old is painful
the word of a brahmin without Vedic recitation is painful

norm.note: a birth-rank norm of the period: a brahmin's word is valued by his Vedic recitation and without it is counted a pain

22.reading: The verse counts four painful things: seeing kings who have no elephants, eating flesh to swell one's own flesh (ranked painful before all), the taste of honey turned sour, and a town cut off by a forest stream.
22.nuance: Each line carries its own intensifier, and முன் 'first, before all' puts the flesh-eater at the head. The other three are things that have lost what makes them work: a king without his elephant force, sweetness gone sour, a town without a road; flesh-eating is filed among them as a corruption of the body's food.

items.claim: seeing kings without elephants is very painful
eating flesh to make one's own flesh grow is painful before all else
the taste of honey once it has soured is painful
a town with a forest river between it and the way is painful

23.reading: The verse counts four painful things: keeping the gate of an old town that has no wall, washing clothes while sitting at the bathing ford, the talk of people who are like a beaten drum, and penance taken up by one without self-restraint.
23.nuance: All four fail for want of the thing that should hold them in: a wall behind the gate, clean water at the ford, a closed mouth, restraint under the penance. அறைபறை அன்னவர் is the Kural's own image for the base who broadcast what they hear (1076).

items.claim: guarding the gate of an old town without a wall is painful
sitting at the ford and washing clothes there is painful
the talk of those who are like a beaten drum is painful
penance undertaken by one without self-restraint is painful

24.reading: The verse counts four painful things: living in an old town without protection, sitting beside people of evil ways, desire grown ripe, which is painful to life itself, and friendship with those who say 'we'.
24.nuance: யாம் என்பவர் 'those who say we' is read here as the self-asserting, who make every bond about themselves; the line could also mean those who merely claim to be one's own. The third item is not desire as such but desire that has ripened (முதிரின்), with harm to உயிர் named.

items.claim: living in an old town without protection is very painful
sitting beside people of evil ways is painful
desire, once it has grown ripe, is painful to life
friendship with those who keep saying 'we' is painful

25.reading: The verse counts four painful things: seeing the troubles of friends, seeing the pride of enemies, dwelling in an old town without order, and gambling with dice one has made one's own.
25.nuance: The first two lines are a pair, the friend brought low and the enemy raised high, both pains of watching. நட்ட கவறு is unclear: from நள் it is dice one has grown attached to, matching நட்டார் 'friends' in line 1; from நடு it would be set or planted dice. The reading of the fourth item depends on which.

items.claim: seeing one's friends in trouble is very painful
seeing the pride of one's enemies is greatly painful
dwelling in an old town without bonds of order is painful
gambling with dice one has become attached to (or set dice) is painful

26.reading: The verse counts four painful things: letting go of a bond tied with the great, saying 'we will do even hard things', telling one's own suffering to those who do not care, and doing evil to the great.
26.nuance: The great open and close the list: first the bond with them let go, last harm done to them, with two faults of speech (the boast, the complaint to the uncaring) between.

items.claim: letting go of a bond tied with the great is painful
saying 'we will do even what is hard' is painful
telling one's suffering to those who do not feel for one is painful
doing evil to the great is painful

27.reading: The verse counts four painful things: destroying the standing of the eminent, casting off those with a close claim on one, beauty in those without means, and falling into old age within youth.
27.nuance: The second line is read with the variant கிழமை யுடையாரை, 'casting off those who have a claim'; as printed (யுடையார்க்கு) the verb is harder to place. இளமையுள் மூப்புப் புகல் may be ageing early or living as the old do while still young.

items.claim: destroying the standing of those who have greatness is painful
casting off those who have a close claim is painful
beauty in those who lack means is painful
entering old age within youth is painful

28.reading: The verse counts four painful things: an unlearned man riding a prancing horse, the worth of words spoken by an incapable man, the grace of speech in the mouths of the poor, and an unlearned man holding an assembly.
28.nuance: The unlearned man frames the verse, on a horse at the start and before an assembly at the end, two kinds of display he cannot carry. Between them speech loses its weight twice, once for want of skill and once for want of wealth.

items.claim: the gallop of a spirited horse ridden by an unlearned man is painful
the yield of words spoken by one without capacity is painful
the grace of speech in the mouths of the poor is painful
an unlearned man holding an assembly is painful

29.reading: The verse counts four painful things: making a great cobra dance without knowing its signs, jumping into water to play without knowing where the stakes stand, begetting children without sense, and a secret heard by one who cannot keep it.
29.nuance: Every item is handling something dangerous without the knowledge it needs; the line on children puts them in that series, so a child without sense is counted with a mishandled snake and a leaked secret.

items.claim: one who does not know the signs making a great snake dance is painful
jumping into water to play without knowing the stakes beneath is painful
getting children who do not come to understanding is painful
a secret heard by one who cannot hold it close is painful

30.reading: The verse counts four painful things: leaping high from the long branch of a tall tree, going against an elephant in fierce rage, a house where a snake lives hidden, and a path where a fierce tiger lives.
30.nuance: This is the one verse of the chapter with no moral item: four plain bodily dangers. It shows the scale the other verses measure faults against.

items.claim: leaping high from the long branch of a tall tree is painful
going to face an elephant in fierce rage is painful
a house in which a snake lives hidden is painful
a path where a fierce tiger lives is painful

31.reading: The verse counts four painful things: singing to a lute not set to its mode, men who cannot reckon telling the days for conduct, the sound of a drum without its clay, and the enmity of those without coolness of temper.
31.nuance: Three items are instruments out of true (an untuned lute, a reckoning without number, a drum without its paste) and the fourth is a person out of true; Kural 573 makes the same move from an unfitted melody to an eye without kindness. The second line is read as an unlettered man fixing auspicious days; the sense is not sure.

items.claim: singing to a lute not set to its mode is greatly painful
men who do not know reckoning declaring the days for conduct is painful
the sound of a drum without its clay paste is painful
the enmity of those who lack coolness of temper is painful

32.reading: The verse counts four painful things: going about without guarding oneself, the backbiting of those who will not speak to one's face, association with those who lack goodness, and the fall of those of ancient standing.
32.nuance: முன்னை உரையார் names the backbiter by what he fails to do, speak in front, so the fault is set against open speech rather than against silence.

items.claim: going about without guarding oneself is very painful
the behind-the-back talk of those who will not speak to one's face is painful
association with those without goodness is painful
the ruin of those of ancient standing is painful

33.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the matter of business a drunkard speaks of, walking in a thorny forest, killing a beast caught in a flood, and association with those of deceitful mind.
33.nuance: The third item faults killing an animal at the moment it is helpless in the flood; the pain lies in the unequal kill, not in hunting as such.

items.claim: the business matter a drunkard speaks of is painful
walking through a thorny forest is very painful
killing a beast caught in a flood is painful
association with those of deceitful mind is painful

34.reading: The verse counts four painful things: speaking of kinship to those without good conduct, even an excellent book to those who do not want it, friendship with people of despised occupation, and a whirling circuit whose sense is obscure.
34.nuance: இழித்த தொழிலவர் ranks people by occupation, and in this period occupation and birth-group largely coincide; the verse does not name the trade, so the line may rank by birth or by base work. The first line has a variant (குறைவுரைத்தல், telling one's wants), and the fourth line (கழிப்புவாய் மண்டிலங் கொட்பு) cannot be fixed: it may be circling at a place of exorcism or at the mouth of a pit.

items.claim: speaking of kinship (or, by a variant, of one's wants) to those without good conduct is painful
even an excellent book is painful to those who do not desire it
friendship with people of a despised occupation is painful
whirling round in a circle at the கழிப்பு place is painful; the sense is unclear

norm.note: a rank norm of the period: friendship with people of a despised occupation is counted a pain

35.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the cloud ceasing its rain for those who live here, a wooden sound sweeter than the flute, illness that befalls small children, and a handsome man who is a fool.
35.nuance: The second line is obscure: as printed it is the sound of wood that should be sweeter than the flute, perhaps a wooden instrument gone harsh; the variant குழலினிய does not settle it. The fourth line counts beauty as a pain when sense is missing, as 27 does when wealth is missing.

items.claim: the rain cloud withholding its rain is painful to those who live here
a wooden sound that should be sweeter than the flute is very painful; the sense is unclear
illness that comes upon small children is painful
a man of beauty being a fool is painful

36.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a man without wealth longing to be liberal, want of money in a city of tall mansions, eating by watching for the houses one may go to, and the friendship of those who desert one at the time of ruin.
36.nuance: The four make a sequence of a falling householder: the wish to give without means, poverty set against a rich city, living off others' doors, and last the friends who leave.

items.claim: a man without wealth desiring to be liberal is painful
lacking money in a long city of tall mansions is painful
eating by waiting on the houses one may come to is painful
the friendship of those who abandon one at the time of ruin is painful

37.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fragrant flower that gives little scent, a man who does not know the ford going down into the water, an ignorant man being questioned, and holding rancour against the small.
37.nuance: Three items expose a lack (scent, knowledge of the ford, an answer); the fourth turns from lack to cruelty, rancour aimed at those weaker than oneself.

items.claim: a fragrant flower not giving its full scent is painful
one who does not know the ford going down into the water is painful
an ignorant man being put to questions is painful
holding rancour against the small is painful

38.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the folly of going after another man's wife, kings without valour entering battle, riding a fierce horse bareback, and work done by one without skill.
38.nuance: The list makes desire for another's wife one of four ventures undertaken without the strength or skill they need, and it uses the Kural's own word for it, பேதைமை (141).

items.claim: the folly of going after another man's wife is painful
kings without valour entering battle is painful
mounting a fierce horse on its bare back is painful
work done by one without skill is painful

39.reading: The verse counts four painful things: liberality in one who has nothing to give, a stone in the areca nut one has bitten, a poet not being sent off by the one who gave to him, and a poet not singing where he has been received.
39.domain_note: the last two items concern patron and poet
39.nuance: The last two lines look at patronage from both sides: the patron who holds the poet back (கொடுத்த விடாமை, tamilvu கொடுத்து விடாமை) and the poet who does not sing when he is taken in. The reading of the third item turns on that printed form.

items.claim: liberality in one with nothing to give is painful
a stone turning up in the areca nut one has bitten is painful
for a poet, not being let go by the one who gives is painful
a poet failing to sing where he has been received is painful

40.reading: The verse counts four painful things: fierce daring in a man of restraint, self-conceit in one without standing, seizing what was left in trust, and the speech of those who will not be checked when checked.
40.nuance: அடக்கம் opens and closes the list: in item 1 the restrained man's martial boldness (மீளிமை) is a pain, perhaps because it is out of his nature or because it is terrible when roused; in item 4 the unrestrainable talker. துடக்கம் in item 2 is read as standing or footing; it may also mean a tie.

items.claim: fierce daring in one who has restraint is painful
self-conceit in one without standing is painful
seizing a deposit left in one's trust is painful
the speech of those who do not subside when checked is painful

links.note: Thirikadugam 18 names old age and great disease as two separate things to fear more than thieves; the Innaa line joins them as one pain, sickness that comes once one is old.
links.teaches: Read together, the two dreads compound: the Innaa line shows disease and age not as two risks but as one in which each makes the other worse.

links.note: Both describe flesh-eating as feeding flesh with flesh (ஊனைப் பெருக்குதல், ஊன் பெருக்கற்கு); the Kural asks how such a person can hold அருள், the Innaa line ranks the act as the first of pains.
links.teaches: The pair shows one image doing two jobs: in the Kural it proves the loss of compassion, in the Innaa verse it is a pain ranked above even soured honey and kingless armies.
links.list_adds: It ranks flesh-eating first (முன்) among things that have lost their proper working, a king without elephants, honey gone sour, a cut-off town.

links.note: The Kural explains the image the Innaa line only names: the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every secret they hear to others.
links.teaches: With the Kural's gloss, the drum-like talker in the Innaa list is seen as a breach of keeping, matching the wall-less gate and the fouled ford beside him.
links.list_adds: It sets loose talk beside a gate with no wall and a ford fouled by washing, so the talker becomes one more failed guard.

links.note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for those without; the Innaa line names what such a man lacks, நிறை, self-restraint.
links.teaches: The Innaa line fills the Kural's circular condition with content: the 'தவம் one must already have' is the inner restraint without which penance is a pain.
links.list_adds: It names the missing quality (நிறை) and files the empty penance with other things whose holding power is gone.

links.note: Verse 23 makes guarding the gate of a wall-less old town painful; 24 makes living in an old town without protection painful.
links.teaches: The second verse moves the pain from the guard's futile labour to the townsman's daily exposure, so one weakness is felt by both its defenders and its dwellers.

links.note: After the town without wall (23) and without protection (24), verse 25 names the old town without கட்டு, bonds of order.
links.teaches: Across three verses the town's weakness moves from its stone to its order, teaching that a town is unsafe for lacking ties as much as for lacking walls.

links.note: Kural 788 defines friendship as clearing a friend's distress at once, like a hand catching a slipping garment; the Innaa line counts the mere sight of a friend's distress as a deep pain.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the feeling behind the Kural's reflex: the friend's hand moves so fast because seeing the trouble already hurts.
links.list_adds: It sets the friend's trouble against the enemy's pride in the next line, so friendship's pain is measured against its mirror in enmity.

links.note: Kural 892 says neglecting the great brings ills through them; the Innaa verse counts doing evil to the great as painful and opens with letting go of a bond with them.
links.teaches: Together they show neglect and injury of the great as stages of one fault, the Innaa list naming the first step, loosening the bond, that the Kural leaves implicit.
links.list_adds: Its first and last items both concern the great, so harming them is shown as the end of a course that begins with letting go of them.

links.note: Iniyavai 28 calls not going about crying for relief from one's distress foremost sweet; the Innaa line calls telling one's suffering to those who do not care painful. They agree from two sides, but the Innaa line narrows the fault to an uncaring listener.
links.teaches: The pair separates self-restraint in grief from the choice of listener: the Iniyavai praises not complaining at all, the Innaa only counts complaint to the indifferent as a pain.

links.note: Iniyavai 37 calls knowing youth as old age sweet; Innaa 27 calls entering old age within youth painful. They do not disagree: one is foresight of age, the other its untimely arrival or imitation.
links.teaches: Read together they keep the counsel to remember age while young from turning into premature decline, the sweet awareness and the painful condition being kept apart.

links.note: Kural 401 likens holding an assembly without full learning to a board game with no board; the Innaa line names the same act, கல்லாதான் கோட்டி கொளல், as painful.
links.teaches: The Innaa verse adds exposure to the Kural's emptiness: paired with the unlearned man on a prancing horse, holding court becomes a display that can throw him.
links.list_adds: It frames the verse with the unlearned man, mounting a spirited horse at the start and holding court at the end, two displays he cannot carry.

links.note: Kural 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when well understood; the Innaa line counts the very grace of speech in a poor man's mouth as painful.
links.teaches: The pair moves the loss from the listeners to the speaker: the Kural notes that no one heeds, the Innaa line that fine speech which cannot land is itself a pain.
links.list_adds: It sets poverty beside want of learning and skill, so wealth and learning appear as the two things that give speech its weight.

links.note: Kural 61 prizes above all children who come to understanding (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு); the Innaa line counts getting children without it (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) as painful.
links.teaches: The Innaa line states the other branch of the Kural's condition, showing that its praise was never of children as such but of children with sense.
links.list_adds: It sets senseless children beside a snake charmed without knowledge and a secret in a careless ear, as power held without the knowledge to handle it.

links.note: 29 counts a secret heard by one who cannot hold it; 23 counts the talk of those who are like a beaten drum.
links.teaches: The two lines describe one leak from both ends, the careless hearer and the broadcasting talker, so the book shows a secret failing first in the ear and then on the tongue.

links.note: Kural 890 makes living with those not in accord like living with a snake in a hut; the Innaa line names the house with a hidden snake plainly, as a bodily danger.
links.teaches: Placed together, the Innaa line gives the literal fear on which the Kural's figure rests, so the reader sees why discord at home is felt as close, quiet and constant danger.
links.list_adds: It keeps the snake-house literal beside a high leap, a raging elephant and a tiger's path, four plain dangers with no moral item.

links.note: Kural 573 asks what use a melody is that does not fit the song, and an eye without kindly regard; the Innaa verse opens with a lute not set to its mode and ends with the enmity of those without coolness.
links.teaches: Both pass from music out of tune to a person out of tune, which suggests a shared idea of kindness as attunement, with the Innaa verse adding enmity as its opposite.
links.list_adds: It spreads the Kural's single analogy over four items, three instruments or reckonings out of true and then a hostile temper.

links.note: Kural 184 grants that harsh words to the face are better than careless words behind the back; the Innaa line names the backbiter as one who will not speak to the face (முன்னை உரையார்).
links.teaches: Both rank the face above the back, and the Innaa wording makes the backbiter's fault a refusal of the open speech the Kural concedes, so cowardice is seen inside the malice.
links.list_adds: It sets backbiting beside failing to guard oneself and bad company, as ways a person is undone without seeing it.

links.note: Iniyavai 34 calls leaving the friendship of worthless people, even when they cling, sweet; the Innaa line calls association with those without goodness painful. The same thing from two sides.
links.teaches: Together they give both the cost and the remedy: the Innaa names the pain of the tie, the Iniyavai the sweetness of cutting it even when the other holds on.

links.note: Kural 929 says giving reasons to a drunk is like searching with a torch for a man under water; the Innaa line says the business a drunkard himself speaks of is painful.
links.teaches: Together they close talk with the drunk in both directions: reasons cannot reach him, and his own account of affairs cannot be relied on.
links.list_adds: It sets the drunk's counsel beside walking on thorns and the deceitful's company, as pains that come through trusting the wrong ground.

links.note: Naladiyar 341 says the base man, though books of weighty meaning are opened for him, goes his own way like a hen scratching rubbish; the Innaa line says even an excellent book is a pain to one who does not want it.
links.teaches: The pair moves the loss from the learner to the teaching: the Naladiyar shows the base mind wasting the book, the Innaa line the book itself suffering a reader who does not want it.
links.list_adds: It sets the unwanted book beside counsel spoken to the unruly and friendship with the despised, all goods given where they do not fit.

links.note: 27 counts beauty in those without means as painful; 35 counts a handsome man who is a fool as painful.
links.teaches: The poet twice makes beauty a pain when what should go with it is missing, wealth in one verse and sense in the other, so beauty is judged by its company.

links.note: Kural 799 says friendship with those who desert one in ruin burns the heart even at death; the Innaa verse closes its run of poverty's pains with the friendship of those who abandon one at the time of ruin.
links.teaches: The Kural measures the desertion by the burn it leaves; the Innaa verse shows it as the last support lost, after the wish to give, the rich city and others' doors have already hurt.
links.list_adds: It places the desertion at the end of a falling householder's sequence, so betrayal is the last stage of poverty, not a separate fault.

links.note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
links.teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.
links.list_adds: It sets the giving wish among the pains of want, a rich city around one and eating at others' doors, so it is seen from inside poverty.

links.note: Iniyavai 22 calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 36 calls longing to be liberal without wealth painful. The same rule seen from two sides: giving should match means.
links.teaches: Together the two books set a measure on liberality, the sweet side naming the rule and the painful side the cost of breaking it.

links.note: Naladiyar 65 says the gift of one without wealth is the true fruit of giving; the Innaa line counts liberality in one who has nothing to give as painful. On the reading that the Naladiyar's giver has little and the Innaa's has nothing, they meet at a limit rather than conflict.
links.teaches: Together they mark where giving from want stops being the highest giving and becomes pain: the point where nothing is left to give.
links.list_adds: It files moneyless liberality with a stone in the chewed areca and broken patronage, as an act that breaks in the middle.

links.note: In Purananuru 101 Avvai tells her heart that whether Athiyaman's gift is delayed or not it is sure, since he greets her on the hundredth visit as on the first; the Innaa line counts a poet held back by the giver as painful.
links.teaches: The poem shows the pain the Innaa line names and how it is borne: a patron's constant welcome makes the delay of the poet's send-off endurable.

links.note: 36 counts a man without wealth longing to be liberal; 39 counts liberality practised by one who has nothing to give.
links.teaches: The poet counts the moneyless giver twice, once in the wish and once in the act, so the pain is not only frustrated desire but the giving itself carried on without means.

links.note: Kural 301 says only restraint of anger where it can take effect counts; the Innaa line counts rancour held against the small as painful.
links.teaches: Read together, anger toward the weak is both the Kural's true test of restraint and the Innaa verse's common failure of it, the same ground seen as trial and as fall.
links.list_adds: It sets rancour toward the weak beside a scentless flower and a fool under questioning, so cruelty is filed with exposures of one's own lack.

links.note: 29 counts jumping into water without knowing the stakes; 37 counts going down into water without knowing the ford.
links.teaches: The poet uses the water twice with two kinds of ignorance, of what lies beneath and of the way in, showing knowledge of place as the condition of entering.

links.note: Both call desire for another man's wife பேதைமை; the Kural says it is absent in those who have seen aram and porul.
links.teaches: The Innaa list explains the shared word by its company: the folly is that of a venture beyond one's strength, like a valourless king in battle, which those the Kural describes would never attempt.
links.list_adds: It sets the folly beside a valourless king in battle, a bareback ride on a fierce horse and unskilled work, so it is ranked as reckless overreach.

links.note: Iniyavai 30 calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit, thinking 'who knew of it then?', the sweetest; Innaa 40 calls seizing a deposit painful. The same thing from two sides.
links.teaches: The Iniyavai line names the thief's private reckoning that no one saw; set against it, the Innaa line shows the betrayal of trust as painful whether or not anyone knew.

links.note: Thirikadugam 62 names the one who wrongfully keeps a deposit among three who live on with their line lost; the Innaa line counts seizing a deposit as painful.
links.teaches: The Thirikadugam names the consequence, loss of descendants, that the Innaa line's bare 'painful' leaves unspoken, so the ethics works together give the act and its price.

source_issues: 21 line 4: ஒத்திலா is read as ஓத்து இலா (without Vedic recitation); the short vowel is likely a misprint.
24 line 4: tamilvu has யாம் என்பவரோடு for யாமென் பவரொடு; the sense is the same.
27 line 2: the printed dative கிழமை யுடையார்க் sits awkwardly with களைந்திடுதல்; the variant கிழமை யுடையாரை is followed.
34 line 1: ஒழுக்க மிலாளார்க் has an unexpected long vowel (variant ஒழுக்கமிலாளர் குறைவுரைத்தல்); line 4 கழிப்புவாய் மண்டிலங் கொட்பு is obscure and its sense cannot be fixed.
35 line 2: the division மரத் தோசை (மரத்து ஓசை) and the variant குழலினிய leave the line's sense unclear.
37 line 3: அறியாண் is likely a misprint for அறியான்.
39 line 3: printed கொடுத்த விடாமை against tamilvu கொடுத்து விடாமை; the reading of the third item turns on it.
